issues.title: Hardcoded RabbitMQ Configuration
issues.description: RabbitMQ host, queue names, and connection details are hardcoded in source code instead of being externalized in configuration files
issues.recommendation: Move RabbitMQ configuration to external configuration files (application.properties or environment variables). Use Azure App Configuration or Key Vault for Azure deployments.
issues.azureMigrationImpact: HIGH - Configuration must be externalized for Azure deployment. Consider using Azure Service Bus as RabbitMQ alternative or Azure Container Apps with RabbitMQ.

issues.title: Outdated Java Version
issues.description: Application targets Java 1.8 (Java 8) which is outdated and no longer receiving public updates
issues.recommendation: Upgrade to Java 11 LTS or Java 17 LTS for better performance, security updates, and Azure support. Java 21 LTS is also recommended.
issues.azureMigrationImpact: MEDIUM - Azure App Service and Azure Container Apps fully support Java 11, 17, and 21. Migration is straightforward.

issues.title: RabbitMQ Dependency for Azure Migration
issues.description: Application uses RabbitMQ which requires additional infrastructure management in Azure
issues.recommendation: Consider migrating to Azure Service Bus for fully managed messaging, or use Azure Container Apps/AKS with RabbitMQ containers. Azure Service Bus provides similar pub/sub capabilities with native Azure integration.
issues.azureMigrationImpact: HIGH - Requires architecture decision between managed Azure Service Bus or containerized RabbitMQ.

issues.title: Embedded Jetty Server
issues.description: Application uses Jetty embedded server which is suitable for development but needs consideration for production Azure deployment
issues.recommendation: For Azure deployment, consider Azure App Service (built-in Tomcat/JBoss), Azure Container Apps, or Azure Kubernetes Service. The WAR file can be deployed to Azure App Service without code changes.
issues.azureMigrationImpact: LOW - Azure App Service supports WAR deployment directly. Minimal changes required.

issues.title: WebSocket Session Management
issues.description: WebSocket sessions are stored in-memory which limits horizontal scalability in Azure
issues.recommendation: For multi-instance deployments in Azure, consider using Azure SignalR Service for WebSocket connections or implement sticky sessions with Azure Application Gateway.
issues.azureMigrationImpact: MEDIUM - Single instance deployment works as-is. Multi-instance requires Azure SignalR Service or sticky sessions.

issues.title: Limited Test Coverage
issues.description: Application has minimal test infrastructure and outdated JUnit version
issues.recommendation: Add comprehensive unit and integration tests. Upgrade to JUnit 5 and add tests for RabbitMQ consumer, WebSocket broadcast, and message publishing.
issues.azureMigrationImpact: LOW - Not a blocker for migration, but important for quality assurance.

issues.title: Maven Build Configuration
issues.description: No Azure-specific build configuration or CI/CD pipeline setup
issues.recommendation: Add Azure DevOps pipeline or GitHub Actions workflow for automated build and deployment. Include Dockerfile for containerized deployment if using Azure Container Apps or AKS.
issues.azureMigrationImpact: HIGH - CI/CD pipeline is essential for Azure deployment automation.

issues.title: Missing Authentication and Authorization
issues.description: No authentication or authorization mechanism implemented for WebSocket endpoints and message publishing
issues.recommendation: Implement Azure Active Directory (AAD) authentication for Azure deployments. Add authorization checks for WebSocket connections and message publishing.
issues.azureMigrationImpact: HIGH - Security is critical for production Azure deployment. Consider Azure AD B2C for user authentication.
